title: Preparing for a New Covenant
subtitle: Building a strong foundation for your second marriage
summary: **You are preparing to make a covenant again.** This is sacred ground. You know now, perhaps more than anyone, that marriage vows are not just words but commitments that shape lives and can end in devastating loss. This journey helps you prepare for remarriage with wisdom, intentionality, and faith. You will examine your readiness, align with your partner on crucial matters, honor what you have learned from your first marriage, and approach this new covenant with both hope and holy seriousness.

cover.heroImageDescription: Two hands joining together with warm light, suggesting both the sacredness of covenant and the hope of new beginnings after loss.

targetOutcomes: Understand the sacred weight of covenant remarriage
Examine your readiness for this commitment
Align with your partner on essential matters
Integrate lessons from your first marriage
Honor your late spouse while fully committing to your new partner
Prepare spiritually for this new chapter

activities.title: Covenant Again: The Weight of What You Are Doing
activities.subtitle: Understanding the sacred seriousness of remarriage
activities.whyThisMatters: You have made marriage vows before and lived their fullness until death parted you. Approaching covenant again requires recognizing both its weight and its hope.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Marriage is a covenant, not merely a contract, and remarriage after widowhood carries unique depth.

cards.title: You Know What This Means
cards.text:
**You are not naive about marriage.**

**You have stood at an altar before and made vows.** You have lived those vows through years of ordinary days and extraordinary challenges. You have loved someone in sickness and in health, for richer and for poorer. And you have experienced what "until death do us part" actually means.

**This gives you something that first-time marriages rarely have: a profound understanding of what you are promising.**

**You know that wedding days end but marriages continue in the mundane moments.** You know that love is not just feeling but choice, repeated daily. You know that two lives woven together create something beautiful and vulnerable. You know that loss is possible.

**Some people rush into marriage with romantic notions.** You cannot. You have lived the reality. You know the weight of what you are about to do.

**This knowledge is not meant to frighten you.** It is meant to ground you. You are entering this covenant with eyes open, with experience earned, with a holy seriousness that honors what marriage actually is.

**"Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it" (Proverbs 4:23|Above all else, guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it).** You are preparing to give your heart again. Guard it well, and give it wisely.

cards.title: Covenant, Not Contract
cards.text:
**Marriage in God's design is a covenant, not a contract.**

**Contracts are transactional.** They specify what each party gives and receives, and they can be dissolved when terms are not met. Contracts protect self-interest.

**Covenants are different.** They are binding commitments that hold regardless of circumstances. They are about giving yourself to another person completely, not keeping score of what you receive in return.

**When you married the first time, you entered a covenant.** You promised yourself to another person unconditionally. That covenant was honored until death ended it, not through failure but through faithful completion.

**Now you are preparing to enter a new covenant.** Different person, different chapter, but the same sacred nature. You will again promise yourself unconditionally. You will again bind your life to another's. You will again say, "Until death do us part," knowing now exactly what those words can mean.

**"So they are no longer two, but one flesh.** Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate" (Matthew 19:6|Until death do us part). God joins. You covenant. This is holy ground.

**Approach it as such.**

cards.title: Hope and Seriousness Together
cards.text:
**The goal of this journey is not to make you somber and scared about remarriage.** It is to help you enter it with both hope and seriousness.

**Hope because God brings good things out of grief.** Because love can bloom again. Because your life is not over, and this new relationship can be a profound blessing.

**Seriousness because you know what is at stake.** Because you have learned that marriage is not something to enter carelessly. Because you want this covenant to be built on a foundation that will last.

**Michael approached his second engagement with a gravity his first engagement lacked.** At twenty-five, he had been naive about what marriage required. At fifty-two, having lost his wife and weathered decades of life, he understood. "I am more serious about this marriage," he said, "because I know what I am promising. And I am more hopeful, because I know what marriage can be."

**Hope and seriousness are not opposites.** They are companions in wisdom.

**"There is surely a future hope for you, and your hope will not be cut off" (Proverbs 23:18|he said).** There is hope. And that hope is worth preparing for well.

cards.title: Your Approach
cards.text: How are you feeling as you prepare for this new covenant? What mix of hope and seriousness do you carry?

cards.title: What You Bring
cards.text:
**Reflect on what you bring to this new covenant from your experience.**

What have you learned about marriage from your first marriage?

What do you understand now about commitment that you did not understand before?

How does having experienced "until death" affect how you approach these vows again?

What hopes do you carry for this new marriage?

What holy seriousness guides your preparation?

**You are not starting from nothing.** You bring wisdom earned through years of marriage and loss.
cards.reflection: What do you bring to this new covenant from your experience of marriage and loss?

cards.title: A Prayer of Preparation
cards.text:
God,

**I am preparing to enter covenant again.** I do not take this lightly.

**I have made these vows before, and I lived them faithfully.** I know what they cost and what they give. I know the weight of promising myself to another person until death.

**I come to You with hope.** Thank You for bringing [partner's name] into my life. Thank You for the possibility of love and companionship again.

**I come to You with seriousness.** Help me prepare well. Show me anything I need to see, address, or understand before I make this covenant.

**Bless this preparation.** Guide my steps. Make me ready for what You are inviting me into.

**"Commit to the Lord whatever you do, and he will establish your plans" (Proverbs 16:3|Commit to the Lord whatever you do, and he will establish your plans).** I commit this engagement, this preparation, this future marriage to You.

Amen.

**Write your own prayer if these words do not fit.**
cards.reflection: **Write your prayer as you begin preparing for this new covenant.**

activities.title: Are You Ready?: Examining Your Heart and Circumstances
activities.subtitle: Honest assessment of your readiness to remarry
activities.whyThisMatters: Being in love is not the same as being ready for marriage. Taking an honest inventory of your readiness protects both you and your partner.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Marriage readiness involves emotional, practical, relational, and spiritual dimensions that should be examined.

cards.title: Love Is Not Enough
cards.text:
**You love this person.** But love alone does not make you ready for marriage.

**Readiness involves many dimensions.** Emotional health. Practical circumstances. Relational alignment. Spiritual foundation. Support systems. Family considerations.

**Many second marriages fail not because love was absent but because readiness was incomplete.** People rush forward on the wings of romance without examining whether the ground beneath them is solid.

**Susan was deeply in love with her fiancé.** But when she honestly examined her readiness, she realized she had not fully grieved her first husband. She was using this new relationship to escape the pain of loss. The love was real, but the timing was wrong. She and her fiancé decided to slow down, giving her time to process her grief before they married. That decision strengthened rather than weakened their relationship.

**Love provides the motivation.** Readiness provides the foundation. You need both.

**"The wise look ahead to see what is coming, but fools deceive themselves" (Proverbs 14:8|The wise look ahead to see what is coming, but fools deceive themselves, NLT).** Look ahead. See what is coming. Do not deceive yourself about your readiness.

cards.title: Grief and Readiness
cards.text:
One crucial question: Have you grieved enough?

**There is no finish line for grief.** You will carry some grief forever, and that is okay. But there is a difference between integrated grief that coexists with new love and unprocessed grief that contaminates it.

Signs that grief may not be sufficiently processed:

**You are using this relationship to escape grief rather than because of genuine love for this person.**

**You cannot talk about your late spouse without intense emotional flooding.**

**You compare your new partner constantly to your late spouse, expecting them to fill that same space.**

**You feel guilty about this relationship, as though you are betraying your late spouse by being happy.**

**You have not addressed practical grief tasks, like going through belongings or adjusting to life alone.**

Signs that grief is sufficiently integrated:

**You can hold both sadness about your loss and joy about your new relationship.**

**Your love for this person is about who they are, not about filling a void.**

**You can speak about your late spouse with appropriate emotion, neither suppressing nor flooding.**

**You feel peace about moving forward, not just desperation to escape loneliness.**

**"He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds" (Psalm 147:3|He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds).** Let Him heal you enough that you bring a whole heart to this new covenant.

cards.title: Other Readiness Factors
cards.text:
**Beyond grief, consider other dimensions of readiness.**

Emotional health: Are you in a good place emotionally? Not perfect, but stable? Have you addressed any mental health concerns?

Practical circumstances: Are finances stable? Living situations workable? Work situations sustainable? Practical chaos makes marriage harder.

Family readiness: If you have children, are they in a place where this transition can work? Have you done the preparation needed with them?

Relational health: Is your relationship with your partner healthy? Have you had conflict and worked through it? Do you communicate well?

Spiritual foundation: Are you both grounded in faith? Is your relationship built on more than just attraction?

Support systems: Do you have people around you who support this marriage? Community that will hold you accountable and encourage you?

**Robert took an honest inventory and realized his financial situation was precarious.** He had been avoiding dealing with it, hoping marriage would somehow solve it. He and his fiancée decided to postpone the wedding until he had addressed the financial issues. It was hard, but it was wise.

**"Suppose one of you wants to build a tower. Won't you first sit down and estimate the cost?" (Luke 14:28|Suppose one of you wants to build a tower.** Won't you first sit down and estimate the cost?). Estimate the cost. Count the factors. Build on solid ground.

cards.title: Your Readiness
cards.text: As you honestly examine yourself, what is your sense of your readiness? What areas feel solid and what areas give you pause?

cards.title: Readiness Inventory
cards.text:
**Take an honest inventory of your readiness.**

Grief: Have you grieved enough? Is your grief integrated rather than unprocessed?

Emotional health: Are you emotionally stable and healthy?

Practical circumstances: Are finances, living situation, and practical matters in order?

Family: Are your children prepared? Have you done the work with them?

Relationship: Is your relationship with your partner healthy and mature?

Faith: Is your spiritual foundation solid?

Support: Do you have community support for this marriage?

**Be honest.** Where are you strong? Where might there be concerns?
cards.reflection: **Complete an honest readiness inventory.** Where are you strong and where are the concerns?

cards.title: Address One Concern
cards.text:
**If your inventory revealed any concerns, choose one to address.**

**If grief is the concern, consider whether you need more time or more intentional grief work before proceeding.**

**If practical matters are the concern, make a plan to address them.** Financial counseling, living arrangement decisions, whatever is needed.

**If family readiness is the concern, focus on preparation with your children.**

**If relationship health is the concern, consider premarital counseling or specific conversations needed.**

**If there are no significant concerns, give thanks and proceed with confidence.**

**Readiness is not about perfection.** It is about honest assessment and appropriate preparation.

**"Prepare your minds for action; be sober-minded" (1 Peter 1:13|Prepare your minds for action; be sober-minded).** Prepare your mind. Be sober. Address what needs addressing.

What will you address?
cards.reflection: What one readiness concern will you address before proceeding?

activities.title: Are You Aligned?: Essential Conversations Before Covenant
activities.subtitle: Making sure you and your partner are on the same page
activities.whyThisMatters: Marriage brings two lives together completely. Alignment on essential matters before the wedding prevents painful surprises after.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Successful marriages require alignment on core values, expectations, and life direction.

cards.title: The Conversations That Matter
cards.text:
Have you had the conversations that matter?

**In the glow of new love, it is easy to assume you are aligned.** You both love each other. You both want to be together. Surely everything else will work out.

**But marriages run into trouble when unspoken assumptions collide with reality.** When you discover too late that you had different expectations about money, or parenting, or where to live, or how to handle conflict.

**These conversations are not romantic.** They can be awkward, even difficult. But they are essential.

**Daniel and his fiancée, Maria, assumed they were aligned because they loved each other deeply.** After marriage, they discovered they had vastly different expectations about finances. He was a saver; she was a spender. He expected transparency; she valued autonomy. The conflict was painful, and they wished they had discussed it before the wedding.

**Do not assume.** Discuss.

**"Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed" (Proverbs 15:22|Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed).** Be counselors to each other. Make plans together. Succeed by talking about what matters.

cards.title: Essential Topics
cards.text:
Topics that require explicit conversation before marriage:

Faith: What role does faith play in your lives? How will you practice it together? Are you aligned spiritually?

Finances: How will you handle money? Joint accounts, separate accounts, both? Who manages what? What are your attitudes toward spending, saving, giving, debt?

Children: How will you parent any children involved? What are your expectations about discipline, roles, and relationships? What if you want different things for them?

Extended family: How will you relate to each other's families? What boundaries are needed? What obligations exist?

Conflict: How do you handle disagreement? Have you seen each other in conflict? Do you resolve or avoid?

Intimacy: What are your expectations about physical intimacy? Any concerns or issues to discuss?

Future: Where will you live? What are your goals? How do you see life unfolding in five, ten, twenty years?

Past: What do you need to know about each other's histories? What baggage might affect your marriage?

**These conversations are your homework before the wedding.** Do not skip them.

**"A person's wisdom yields patience; it is to one's glory to overlook an offense" (Proverbs 19:11|A person's wisdom yields patience; it is to one's glory to overlook an offense).** Have patient, wise conversations. Work through offenses before they become marriage problems.

cards.title: Premarital Counseling
cards.text:
**Strongly consider premarital counseling.**

**A skilled counselor or pastor can guide you through important conversations you might avoid on your own.** They can identify potential issues you have not seen. They can give you tools for communication and conflict resolution that will serve you for decades.

**This is especially valuable for second marriages.** You bring more complexity: previous marriage patterns, grief, possibly children, established lives being merged. A counselor helps navigate this complexity.

**Linda and her fiancé, James, were both independent people who had lived alone for years.** Premarital counseling helped them see how their independence could become a problem if they did not learn to make space for togetherness. The counselor gave them exercises that helped them practice interdependence before the wedding.

**Premarital counseling is not remedial.** It is not for couples with problems. It is wisdom for any couple who wants to start strong.

**"Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety" (Proverbs 11:14|Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety).** Get guidance. Find safety in counsel.

cards.title: Your Alignment
cards.text: How aligned do you feel with your partner on essential matters? What conversations have you had, and what conversations might still be needed?

cards.title: Conversation Checklist
cards.text:
**Review the essential conversation topics and assess where you stand.**

Faith: Have you discussed this? Are you aligned?

Finances: Have you discussed this? Are you aligned?

Children and parenting: Have you discussed this? Are you aligned?

Extended family: Have you discussed this? Are you aligned?

Conflict resolution: Have you discussed this? Have you experienced conflict and seen how you resolve it?

Intimacy: Have you discussed this? Are you aligned?

Future plans: Have you discussed this? Are you aligned?

Past and baggage: Have you discussed this? Does your partner know what they need to know?

Which topics need more conversation?
cards.reflection: Which essential topics still need conversation with your partner?

cards.title: Have One Essential Conversation
cards.text:
**Choose one essential topic and have a deep conversation about it with your partner this week.**

**Pick a topic you have not fully discussed or where you sense there might be unspoken assumptions.**

**Set aside uninterrupted time.** This is not a car conversation. It is a sit-down, face-to-face, phones-away conversation.

**Ask open questions.** "What do you think about...?" "How do you imagine we would handle...?" "What are your expectations about...?"

**Listen as much as you talk.** The goal is mutual understanding, not winning.

**If you discover misalignment, do not panic.** Discuss it. Work through it. Better now than after the wedding.

Also consider: Have you done or scheduled premarital counseling? If not, make that a priority.

**"Let the wise listen and add to their learning, and let the discerning get guidance" (Proverbs 1:5|Let the wise listen and add to their learning, and let the discerning get guidance).** Be wise. Listen. Get guidance.

What conversation will you have?
cards.reflection: What essential conversation will you have with your partner this week?

activities.title: What You Learned: Bringing Wisdom from Your First Marriage
activities.subtitle: Integrating lessons from your marriage experience
activities.whyThisMatters: Your first marriage taught you things you could not have learned any other way. Bringing that wisdom into your new marriage is a gift of your experience.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Prior marriage experience provides wisdom that can strengthen subsequent marriages when intentionally applied.

cards.title: Hard-Won Wisdom
cards.text:
**Your first marriage gave you an education that no book or class could provide.**

**You learned what works in marriage and what does not.** What brings connection and what creates distance. How to love someone through difficulty and how conflict can erode or strengthen a bond.

**You learned about yourself as a spouse.** Your strengths, your weaknesses, your patterns. How you show up when things are good and how you respond when they are not.

**This wisdom was earned over years, through joys and struggles, through getting it right sometimes and getting it wrong other times.** It is invaluable.

**Bringing this wisdom into your new marriage is one of the gifts of marrying with experience.** You do not have to repeat old mistakes. You can build on what you learned.

**Carol realized that in her first marriage, she had been conflict-avoidant, letting small issues build into large resentments.** In her second marriage, she committed to addressing things early. "I learned that the hard way," she said. "I am not making that mistake again."

**"Wisdom is more precious than rubies, and nothing you desire can compare with her" (Proverbs 8:11|I learned that the hard way).** You have gained wisdom. It is precious. Use it.

cards.title: What Your Marriage Taught You
cards.text:
**Reflect on the specific lessons your first marriage taught.**

About communication: What did you learn about how to talk to a spouse, how to listen, how to be heard?

About conflict: What did you learn about handling disagreement, fighting fair, repairing after hurt?

About intimacy: What did you learn about emotional and physical closeness, maintaining connection, keeping romance alive?

About partnership: What did you learn about sharing life, making decisions together, supporting each other's growth?

About yourself: What did you learn about your own needs, patterns, strengths, and weaknesses as a spouse?

About what matters: What did you learn about what is truly important in marriage and what is trivial?

**Joseph learned from his first marriage that quality time was essential for his wife to feel loved.** He had not understood that at first and had prioritized work over presence. In his second marriage, he was intentional about time from the beginning.

**"The heart of the discerning acquires knowledge, for the ears of the wise seek it out" (Proverbs 18:15|The heart of the discerning acquires knowledge, for the ears of the wise seek it out).** You have acquired knowledge. Now apply it.

cards.title: Patterns to Change
cards.text:
**Some lessons from your first marriage may be about patterns you need to change.**

**Every marriage has two contributors.** Even in a good marriage, you were not a perfect spouse. There may be patterns, habits, or tendencies that you want to do differently this time.

**Maybe you were too passive or too controlling.** Maybe you withdrew when you should have engaged or fought when you should have let things go. Maybe you neglected your spouse's needs or forgot to express appreciation.

**Be honest about your part.** Not to condemn yourself but to grow. What would you do differently if you could?

**This is not dishonoring your late spouse.** They would want you to become a better person, a better spouse. Learning from what did not work honors the relationship by using it for growth.

**Evelyn knew she had been critical in her first marriage.** She had seen problems more than blessings, had pointed out flaws more than expressed gratitude. She worked intentionally to cultivate appreciation in her second marriage, training herself to notice and express the positive.

**"Search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts. See if there is any offensive way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting" (Psalm 139:23-24|Search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts.** See if there is any offensive way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting). Let God search your heart. Let Him show you what to change.

cards.title: Your Lessons
cards.text: What are the most important lessons you learned from your first marriage that you want to bring into this one?

cards.title: Wisdom Inventory
cards.text:
**Take inventory of the wisdom you bring from your first marriage.**

What worked well that you want to continue or repeat?

What did not work that you want to avoid or do differently?

What did you learn about yourself as a spouse that informs how you want to show up in this marriage?

What did your late spouse teach you about being loved or loving well?

What patterns do you want to change?

What commitments do you want to make based on what you learned?
cards.reflection: What wisdom from your first marriage will you bring into this one? What will you do differently?

cards.title: Share Your Lessons
cards.text:
**Share some of what you have learned with your partner.**

**This is vulnerable.** You are talking about your previous marriage, about your own failures and growth, about what you learned the hard way.

**But it is also bonding.** It lets your partner know who you are becoming, what you are committed to, how your experience has shaped you.

Consider sharing:

**"Something I learned from my first marriage that I want to bring into ours is.**.."

**"Something I did not do well before that I am committed to doing better is.**.."

**"Something my late spouse taught me about love that I carry with me is.**.."

**This conversation honors your past while committing to your future.** It brings your wisdom into your shared preparation.

**"A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in a setting of silver" (Proverbs 25:11).** Speak fitting words to your partner. Share the gold you have gained.

When will you have this conversation?
cards.reflection: What will you share with your partner about what you learned from your first marriage?

activities.title: Two Loves: Honoring Your Past While Embracing Your Future
activities.subtitle: Navigating the complexity of loving again
activities.whyThisMatters: You will always love your late spouse and you are committing to love someone new. Navigating both loves with integrity is part of this new covenant.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Widowed individuals must integrate continuing love for deceased spouse with full commitment to new partner.

cards.title: You Will Always Love Them
cards.text:
**Let us be clear about something: you will always love your late spouse.**

**Marrying again does not end that love.** It does not erase it, replace it, or diminish it. The love you shared is part of you forever. It lives in your memories, in who you have become, in the life you built together.

**This is not a problem to be solved.** It is a reality to be honored.

**Some people feel they must stop loving their late spouse to fully love someone new.** This is not true. The human heart has more capacity than that. You can love someone who is gone and someone who is present. These loves are not in competition.

**Andrew worried that his love for his late wife meant he could not fully commit to his fiancée.** His pastor helped him understand: "Your love for Janet is a chapter of your story that is complete. Your love for Michelle is a new chapter. Both are real. Both are good. The book holds them both."

**You do not have to stop loving to love again.** You carry the old love as you build the new one.

**"Love never fails" (1 Corinthians 13:8|Your love for Janet is a chapter of your story that is complete. Your love for Michelle is a new chapter. Both are real. Both are good. The book holds them both.).** Your love for your late spouse has not failed. And your love for your new partner is also enduring.

cards.title: Full Commitment to Your Partner
cards.text:
**While you will always love your late spouse, your new partner deserves your full commitment.**

**This is the covenant tension.** You honor the past while being fully present to the future. You carry one love while giving another.

Full commitment means:

**Your new partner is not second best.** They are not a consolation prize or a substitute. They are the one you are choosing now, fully and completely.

**They get your full heart, not your leftovers.** Yes, part of your heart holds your late spouse, but the part that is about daily love, about presence, about future building, belongs to your new partner.

**You do not compare.** Your late spouse and your new partner are different people. Comparing is unfair to everyone.

**You are present.** When you are with your partner, you are with them. Not lost in memories of someone else.

**Rachel made a commitment to herself: when she was with Thomas, she would be fully with Thomas.** She could grieve her late husband at other times, but their time together belonged to their relationship. This was not suppressing her grief. It was honoring both relationships appropriately.

**"Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart" (Colossians 3:23|Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart).** Work at this marriage with all your heart. Give it your full self.

cards.title: Your Partner and Your Past
cards.text:
**Your new partner has to navigate your past too.** This requires grace from both of you.

**They may feel insecure sometimes, wondering if they measure up, if you wish your late spouse were here instead, if they will always be in someone's shadow.**

**They may need reassurance.** They may need to hear that they are loved for themselves, chosen completely, not just filling a void.

**At the same time, they need to accept that your late spouse is part of your story.** A secure partner does not compete with a memory but honors it as part of who you are.

**Open conversation helps.** "I want you to know that my love for [late spouse] does not take anything from my love for you. You are not competing with anyone. You are who I am choosing, fully."

**David's fiancée sometimes felt the presence of his late wife in their relationship, in photos around the house, in stories he told, in grief that surfaced.** David learned to reassure her regularly: "You are not second. You are who I want to spend my life with now. She was then; you are now. Both are real, and I choose you."

**"Therefore encourage one another and build each other up" (1 Thessalonians 5:11|You are not second. You are who I want to spend my life with now. She was then; you are now. Both are real, and I choose you.).** Build up your partner. Encourage them. Help them feel secure in your love.

cards.title: Your Two Loves
cards.text: How are you navigating the relationship between your continuing love for your late spouse and your commitment to your new partner?

cards.title: Honoring and Committing
cards.text:
**Reflect on how you will honor your past while fully committing to your future.**

How will you continue to honor your late spouse's memory in your new marriage? What practices will you maintain?

How will you ensure your new partner feels fully loved and chosen, not second best?

What boundaries might help? Times for grief, times for presence with your partner?

What conversations do you need to have with your partner about navigating this?

How will you handle moments when grief surfaces during your marriage?
cards.reflection: How will you honor your late spouse while fully committing to your new partner?

cards.title: A Commitment to Your Partner
cards.text:
**Make a commitment to your partner about how you will navigate your two loves.**

**I will always honor [late spouse's name].** They were part of my life, and they shaped who I am. I will not pretend they did not exist or that I did not love them.

**And I commit to you fully.** You are not a replacement. You are not second. You are the person I am choosing now, completely.

**I commit to being present with you, not lost in the past when we are together.**

**I commit to reassuring you when you need it, helping you feel secure in my love.**

**I commit to building a life with you that is ours, not a copy of what I had before.**

**I carry two loves.** But my covenant is with you.

**Consider sharing this commitment with your partner.** Let them hear your words.

**"Let love and faithfulness never leave you; bind them around your neck, write them on the tablet of your heart" (Proverbs 3:3|Let love and faithfulness never leave you; bind them around your neck, write them on the tablet of your heart).** Bind love and faithfulness together. For your late spouse and for your new partner.

What will you commit to?
cards.reflection: What commitment will you make to your partner about navigating your two loves?

activities.title: Blending Lives: Preparing for a Combined Household
activities.subtitle: Practical and relational preparation for merging lives
activities.whyThisMatters: Remarriage often means blending households, children, traditions, and ways of life. Preparing for this complexity sets your family up for success.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Blended families require intentional preparation and realistic expectations about the integration process.

cards.title: More Than Two People
cards.text:
**When you marry, you are not just joining two people.** You are blending lives, histories, and possibly children.

**This is significantly more complex than a first marriage between two people without prior families.** You bring established patterns, existing relationships, and formed identities. Merging these takes intention and time.

**If children are involved, the complexity multiplies.** You are not just becoming spouses; you are forming a new family system with all its dynamics.

**This does not mean it cannot work.** Blended families can be deeply satisfying and loving. But they require realistic expectations about the adjustment process.

**Terrence and his wife thought the hard part was getting to the wedding.** They discovered afterward that blending their two families, his two kids and her three, was the real work. The first two years were harder than they expected. But they persisted, and eventually the family became genuinely bonded.

**"Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain" (Psalm 127:1|Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain).** You are building a house. Let the Lord build it. And be prepared for the labor it requires.

cards.title: Practical Blending
cards.text:
**Consider the practical dimensions of blending your lives.**

Living situation: Where will you live? Whose house? Will you find a new place together? How do the practical logistics work?

Finances: How will you merge or manage finances? What assets and debts does each person bring? What approach to money will you use as a couple?

Household management: Who does what? How are chores divided? What are the expectations about how the home runs?

Schedules: How do your schedules work together? Work times, children's activities, regular commitments?

Traditions: What traditions does each person or family bring? How will you blend or create new ones?

Space: How will personal space work? Where are the boundaries? What remains individual and what becomes shared?

**These practical matters may seem mundane, but they are where daily life happens.** Getting them right matters.

**Gloria and her fiancé created a detailed plan for their first year of blended household life.** Who was responsible for what, how finances would work, what the schedule would look like. The plan needed adjustments, but having a starting framework reduced chaos.

**"The plans of the diligent lead to profit" (Proverbs 21:5|The plans of the diligent lead to profit).** Be diligent in planning. It will profit your household.

cards.title: Relational Blending
cards.text:
**Beyond the practical, there is relational blending.**

**You and your partner need to establish your relationship as the center of the family.** This is the foundation. If the marriage is strong, the family has a chance. If the marriage is weak, the family will struggle.

**If children are involved, the stepparent relationships need ongoing nurture.** These do not happen automatically and often take years to fully develop.

**Extended families must be navigated.** In-laws, grandparents, former in-laws, all have relationships with your children and opinions about your marriage.

**Friendships may shift.** Some friends may not fit into your blended life the way they did before.

**All of this relational adjustment takes time and energy.** Expect it. Budget for it. Do not be surprised when it is hard.

**Patrick found that his relationship with his new wife's parents was awkward.** They had loved their son-in-law who died and were slow to accept Patrick. He had to be patient, not forcing relationship, letting trust build over years.

**"Be completely humble and gentle; be patient, bearing with one another in love" (Ephesians 4:2|Be completely humble and gentle; be patient, bearing with one another in love).** Be humble. Be patient. Bear with one another. This is how relational blending happens.

cards.title: Your Blending Challenges
cards.text: What are the biggest blending challenges you anticipate? What practical or relational complexities do you see ahead?

cards.title: Blending Preparation
cards.text:
**Think through what blending your lives will require.**

Practically: What decisions need to be made about living situation, finances, household management, schedules?

With children (if applicable): What do your children need as this family forms? What preparation have you done with them?

Relationally: What relationships need attention? Your marriage, stepparent relationships, extended family, friendships?

What do you expect to be easy? What do you expect to be hard?

What conversations or plans do you and your partner still need to have?
cards.reflection: What preparation do you need for blending your lives? What decisions and conversations are needed?

cards.title: A Blending Conversation
cards.text:
**Have a conversation with your partner about one aspect of blending your lives.**

**Pick an area that needs attention: living situation, finances, household management, children, extended family, or something else.**

**Do not try to solve everything.** Focus on one area.

Discuss: What are we thinking? What are our assumptions? What decisions need to be made? What might be difficult?

**Make a plan or identify next steps.** What will you do with what you discussed?

**Blending is not figured out in one conversation.** But each conversation moves you forward.

**"Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor" (Ecclesiastes 4:9|Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor).** Work together. Your labor will have good return.

What blending topic will you discuss?
cards.reflection: What aspect of blending will you discuss with your partner this week?

activities.title: Built on Rock: Establishing Your Spiritual Foundation
activities.subtitle: Grounding your new marriage in faith
activities.whyThisMatters: A marriage built on spiritual foundation has resources to draw on when times are hard. Establishing that foundation before the wedding is wisdom.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Shared spiritual foundation provides strength, meaning, and resources for marriage challenges.

cards.title: Rock or Sand
cards.text:
**Jesus told a parable about two builders.** One built on rock; the other built on sand. When the storms came, the house on rock stood while the house on sand fell.

**Your marriage will face storms.** Every marriage does. The question is what foundation you have built on.

**A marriage built on attraction alone is sand.** Attraction fades and changes. A marriage built on convenience is sand. Circumstances shift. A marriage built on need is sand. Needs can be met elsewhere.

**A marriage built on shared faith is rock.** Faith provides meaning when life is hard, resources when you are depleted, a framework for forgiveness and grace, a third party, God Himself, who holds you both.

**This does not mean faith makes marriage easy.** It means faith gives you something solid to stand on when marriage is hard.

**Kenneth and his fiancée made their faith the foundation of their relationship from the beginning.** They prayed together, attended church together, and talked about how faith would shape their marriage. When they hit hard times two years in, that foundation held them.

**"Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and puts them into practice is like a wise man who built his house on the rock" (Matthew 7:24|Therefore everyone who hears these words of mine and puts them into practice is like a wise man who built his house on the rock).** Build on rock. Put His words into practice. Be wise.

cards.title: Shared Spiritual Practices
cards.text:
**Consider what spiritual practices will be part of your marriage.**

**Praying together: Regular times of praying as a couple.** This builds intimacy with God and with each other.

**Church involvement: Worshiping together, being part of a faith community, serving alongside each other.**

**Scripture: Reading the Bible together, discussing what you learn, applying it to your life and marriage.**

**Spiritual conversations: Talking about faith, about what God is doing in your lives, about how to navigate decisions in light of your beliefs.**

**Shared values: Living out your faith through how you treat people, how you use money, how you raise children, how you handle conflict.**

**You may come from different faith backgrounds or have different styles of spirituality.** Discuss this. Find what you can share. Build practices that work for both of you.

**Natalie and her fiancé had different church backgrounds.** Rather than fight about whose tradition was right, they found a church that felt like home to both of them and built their shared spiritual life there.

**"Though one may be overpowered, two can defend themselves. A cord of three strands is not quickly broken" (Ecclesiastes 4:12|Though one may be overpowered, two can defend themselves.** A cord of three strands is not quickly broken). The third strand is God. Weave Him into your marriage.

cards.title: When You Differ
cards.text:
What if you and your partner are not perfectly aligned spiritually?

**This is common and not necessarily disqualifying.** But it requires honest conversation and realistic expectations.

**If one of you is deeply committed to faith and the other is not, this is significant.** The gap may cause friction throughout your marriage. Discuss it honestly before proceeding.

**If you share faith but differ on details, such as different denominations or theological views, find common ground.** Focus on what unites you rather than what divides.

**Be clear about expectations.** Will you attend the same church? How will you raise children spiritually? What practices are non-negotiable for each of you?

**Do not assume the other person will change.** Marry them as they are, not as you hope they will become.

**Benjamin was more devout than his fiancée.** They discussed it openly. She respected his faith and was willing to participate in church, even though it was not as central to her. They agreed on how to raise children spiritually. The honesty about their differences prevented later disappointment.

**"Do not be yoked together with unbelievers" (2 Corinthians 6:14|Do not be yoked together with unbelievers).** This verse calls for wisdom. Know where you align and where you differ. Make informed choices.

cards.title: Your Spiritual Foundation
cards.text: What is the spiritual foundation of your relationship? How aligned are you and your partner in faith?

cards.title: Building Spiritual Foundation
cards.text:
**Assess and plan your spiritual foundation.**

How would you describe your individual faith? Your partner's faith?

Where are you aligned spiritually? Where do you differ?

What spiritual practices do you currently share? What would you like to add?

How will faith be expressed in your marriage? In your home? In how you make decisions?

If you have differences, how will you navigate them?

What conversations do you need to have about the spiritual foundation of your marriage?
cards.reflection: What spiritual foundation will you build your marriage on? What practices and commitments?

cards.title: Establish One Practice
cards.text:
**Choose one spiritual practice to establish in your relationship before the wedding.**

**If you do not already pray together regularly, start.** Even a brief prayer at the end of time together establishes the habit.

**If you are not attending church together, start.** Make it part of your shared rhythm.

**If you have not discussed your spiritual values and expectations, have that conversation.**

**If you have not read Scripture together, try it.** Start with a short passage and discuss it.

**One practice, established now, creates a foundation you can build on throughout your marriage.**

**"But seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well" (Matthew 6:33|But seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well).** Seek Him first. Together. Let everything else flow from that.

What practice will you establish?
cards.reflection: What spiritual practice will you establish with your partner before the wedding?

activities.title: Words That Bind: Preparing Your Vows
activities.subtitle: Crafting promises that reflect your journey and commitment
activities.whyThisMatters: Vows are the words that create the covenant. For someone who has made and kept vows before, these words carry profound weight.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Marriage vows in remarriage carry particular significance given the experience of having lived vows before.

cards.title: You Know These Words Are Real
cards.text:
**When you said your first wedding vows, you meant them.** But you may not have fully understood them.

**For better or worse sounded nice but abstract.** In sickness and in health was a line to repeat, not a reality you had lived. Until death do us part was a distant someday, not something that would actually happen.

**Now you know.** You have lived these words. You have experienced the worse and the sickness and the death. You know that vows are not poetry. They are promises that shape and cost and demand everything.

**This knowledge makes your new vows different.** They are not naive promises made by someone who does not understand. They are deliberate commitments made by someone who knows exactly what they mean.

**Melissa said that writing her second wedding vows made her cry in a way her first vows had not.** "I knew what I was promising this time. I had lived it. These words were not just words anymore. They were my life."

**"When you make a vow to God, do not delay to fulfill it.** He has no pleasure in fools; fulfill your vow" (Ecclesiastes 5:4|I knew what I was promising this time. I had lived it. These words were not just words anymore. They were my life.). You are making a vow. Make it carefully. Make it truly. Fulfill it completely.

cards.title: What to Include
cards.text:
**Whether you write your own vows or use traditional ones, consider what should be included.**

**Commitment: Clear statement of your promise.** You are binding yourself to this person.

**Scope: For better or worse, richer or poorer, sickness and health.** These are not just phrases. You have lived them. Mean them.

**Duration: Until death.** You know what this means now. Say it knowing.

**Before God: Marriage is a covenant witnessed by God.** Acknowledge His presence and authority.

You may also want to include:

**Acknowledgment of your journey: How you have come through loss to this place of new love.**

**Promises specific to your relationship: What you commit to this particular person.**

**Recognition of family: If children are involved, you might include commitment to them.**

**Traditional vows have endured because they say what needs to be said.** Personal vows can add meaning specific to your story. Either way, let the words carry the weight they deserve.

**"Let your 'Yes' be 'Yes,' and your 'No,' 'No'" (Matthew 5:37|Let your 'Yes' be 'Yes,' and your 'No,' 'No').** Let your vows be true. Let them mean what they say.

cards.title: Vows That Reflect Your Journey
cards.text:
**Your vows can reflect the unique journey you have taken.**

**You can acknowledge loss without dwelling on it.** Something as simple as: "Having known love and loss, I come to you with a full heart."

**You can honor the wisdom you bring.** "I bring what I have learned about love, and I promise to love you with all I have become."

**You can name your choice.** "I choose you, not to replace what was, but to build something new."

**You can commit with full knowledge.** "I know what these vows mean. I have lived them. And I make them to you freely and completely."

**Thomas included in his vows: "I have walked through the valley of the shadow of death.** And I have found, on the other side, you. I do not take this lightly. I know what I am promising. And I promise it with my whole heart."

**Your journey matters.** Let your vows reflect it.

**"The tongue has the power of life and death" (Proverbs 18:21|I have walked through the valley of the shadow of death. And I have found, on the other side, you. I do not take this lightly. I know what I am promising. And I promise it with my whole heart.).** Your vows speak life into your marriage. Choose words that carry the meaning you intend.

cards.title: Your Vows
cards.text: What do you want your vows to express? What is essential for you to promise?

cards.title: Preparing Your Vows
cards.text:
**Spend time preparing what you will vow.**

What do you want to promise? What commitments are essential?

How do you want to reflect your journey in your vows?

What specific promises do you want to make to this particular person?

What do traditional vows include that you want to preserve?

If you are writing personal vows, what tone do you want? Serious, tender, hopeful?

If children are involved, will you include any commitment to them?
cards.reflection: What do you want to promise? How will your vows reflect your journey and commitment?

cards.title: Draft Your Vows
cards.text:
**Begin drafting your vows.**

**If you are using traditional vows, read through them slowly.** Let each phrase sink in. Consider what it means, what it will cost, what you are promising.

**If you are writing personal vows, write a first draft.** Do not edit yet. Just let the words flow. What do you want to say? What does your heart want to promise?

**If you are uncertain what approach to take, discuss with your partner.** Will you use traditional vows, write your own, or combine approaches?

**Let these words matter.** They will be the foundation of your covenant.

**"May these words of my mouth and this meditation of my heart be pleasing in your sight, Lord, my Rock and my Redeemer" (Psalm 19:14|May these words of my mouth and this meditation of my heart be pleasing in your sight, Lord, my Rock and my Redeemer).** Let your vows please Him. Let them honor your partner. Let them mean everything.

When will you work on your vows?
cards.reflection: When will you draft your vows? What will you include?

activities.title: The Day Itself: Preparing for Your Wedding
activities.subtitle: Making your wedding meaningful and honoring
activities.whyThisMatters: Your wedding day is a sacred celebration. Preparing for it with intention ensures it honors your journey, your commitment, and the God who has brought you here.

frameworkBasis.explanation: The wedding ceremony and celebration should reflect the sacredness of the covenant being made.

cards.title: A Different Kind of Wedding
cards.text:
**Your wedding will likely be different from your first one.**

**You are different.** You have lived, loved, lost, and grown. A first wedding's wide-eyed innocence is replaced by an experienced commitment.

**Circumstances may be different.** You may have children to include. You may be older, with different priorities about celebration. Your community of family and friends has shifted.

**Expectations may be different.** A smaller ceremony may feel right. A more intimate celebration. Or perhaps you want a full celebration precisely because you know how precious this is.

**There is no right way to do a second wedding.** Some are large and joyful. Some are small and intimate. What matters is that it reflects who you are and the seriousness of what you are doing.

**Victoria had a big first wedding.** For her second, she and her fiancé chose a small ceremony with just family and close friends. "It felt more us," she said. "Less about the party and more about the promise."

**"There is a time for everything.**.. a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance" (Ecclesiastes 3:1|It felt more us,, 4). This is a time to celebrate. Do it in a way that fits you.

cards.title: Honoring the Past at Your Wedding
cards.text:
**You may wonder whether or how to acknowledge your late spouse at your wedding.**

**There is no universal answer.** Some people want no mention, keeping the day focused entirely on the new marriage. Others want some acknowledgment of the journey that brought them here.

Options for acknowledgment:

**A moment of silence or prayer for loved ones who have passed.**

**A small memorial, such as a candle or photo, in a side area rather than center stage.**

**Mention in the ceremony by the officiant, brief and honoring.**

**A private ritual before the ceremony, visiting a grave or saying a personal goodbye to that chapter.**

**Consider your partner's comfort.** This is their wedding too. Any acknowledgment should feel right to both of you.

**Consider your children's needs.** If your children are grieving their parent, some acknowledgment may help them feel that parent is not being erased.

**Frank and his fiancée included a moment of silence for "loved ones who are not with us today.**" It was brief, tender, and meaningful without making his late wife the focus of a day that belonged to his new marriage.

**"Honor one another above yourselves" (Romans 12:10|loved ones who are not with us today.**).** Honor your late spouse appropriately. Honor your new partner completely. Find the balance.

cards.title: Making It Sacred
cards.text:
**Whatever form your wedding takes, let it be sacred.**

**Sacred means set apart, significant, touched by the holy.** Your wedding is not just a party. It is a covenant made before God and witnesses.

**Include God explicitly.** Prayer, Scripture, blessing by a minister or faith community. Let the ceremony make clear that this is a spiritual act.

**Make the vows central.** Everything else is decoration. The vows are the point. Give them weight in how you structure the ceremony.

**Include your community.** Witnesses matter. Having people present who will support your marriage, who will hold you accountable, who will celebrate and sustain you.

**Be present.** On the day itself, amid all the activity, take moments to be fully present. This is the day you enter covenant. Do not miss it.

**Amanda and her husband wrote a prayer together that they prayed aloud at the end of their ceremony, dedicating their marriage to God.** It grounded the day in something bigger than themselves.

**"Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain" (Psalm 127:1|Unless the Lord builds the house, the builders labor in vain).** Let the Lord build this house. Let your wedding be the groundbreaking ceremony for His work.

cards.title: Your Wedding Plans
cards.text: What are your hopes for your wedding day? What do you want it to look and feel like?

cards.title: Wedding Preparation
cards.text:
**Think through what you want for your wedding.**

What kind of ceremony do you envision? Large or small? Formal or casual? Traditional or unique?

How will faith be expressed in the ceremony? Prayer, Scripture, blessing, other?

Will you acknowledge your late spouse in any way? How will you balance honoring the past with celebrating the future?

How will children be included if they are part of your family?

What elements are most important to you? What could you let go?

What do you want to remember about this day?
cards.reflection: What do you want for your wedding? What matters most?

cards.title: Plan One Element
cards.text:
**Focus on one element of your wedding this week.**

**If the ceremony structure needs attention, work on that.** Talk to your officiant. Decide on the flow.

**If you have not decided about acknowledging your late spouse, make that decision with your partner.**

**If including children needs planning, focus there.**

**If the spiritual elements need thought, decide what prayer, Scripture, or blessing will be included.**

**Wedding planning has many moving parts.** Focus on one that matters to you.

**"Commit to the Lord whatever you do, and he will establish your plans" (Proverbs 16:3|Commit to the Lord whatever you do, and he will establish your plans).** Commit your planning to Him. He will establish it.

What element will you focus on?
cards.reflection: What one element of wedding planning will you focus on this week?

activities.title: Entering Covenant: Final Preparation and Blessing
activities.subtitle: Standing on the threshold of your new marriage
activities.whyThisMatters: You are about to make a sacred covenant. This final activity is a blessing and commissioning as you prepare to say "I do" again.

frameworkBasis.explanation: Entering covenant benefits from intentional blessing and spiritual preparation.

cards.title: You Have Prepared Well
cards.text:
**You have done significant preparation for this covenant.**

**You have examined your readiness, looking honestly at grief, emotions, circumstances, and relationships.**

**You have aligned with your partner on essential matters, having conversations that many couples never have.**

**You have brought wisdom from your first marriage, learning from what worked and what you want to do differently.**

**You have navigated the complexity of loving again, honoring your past while committing to your future.**

**You have prepared for blending lives and establishing spiritual foundation.**

**You have crafted vows that carry the weight they deserve and planned a wedding that honors the sacred nature of what you are doing.**

**This preparation is a gift to your marriage.** You are not entering covenant carelessly. You are entering with eyes open, heart prepared, and foundation laid.

**"The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but victory rests with the Lord" (Proverbs 21:31|The horse is made ready for the day of battle, but victory rests with the Lord).** You have made ready. Victory rests with Him. Trust Him as you enter.

cards.title: What You Are About to Do
cards.text:
**In a short time, you will stand before God and witnesses and make a covenant.**

**You will promise yourself to another person completely.** You will bind your life to theirs. You will create a new family, a new household, a new entity that did not exist before.

**This is profound.** This is sacred. This deserves a moment of holy pause.

**You have been here before.** You know what comes after the wedding day, the ordinary days, the challenges, the deep joys, the disappointments, the growth, the moments when love is a feeling and the moments when love is only a choice.

**You also know, in a way many do not, that this covenant will end.** Either through death or through something worse. You cannot know when or how. But you know that "until death" is not theoretical. It is real.

**This knowledge does not diminish your commitment.** It deepens it. You are choosing this with full knowledge of what it means and what it costs.

**"Place me like a seal over your heart, like a seal on your arm; for love is as strong as death" (Song of Songs 8:6|is not theoretical. It is real. **This knowledge does not diminish your commitment. It deepens it. You are choosing this with full knowledge of what it means and what it costs. **).** Love is as strong as death. You know both. Enter this love with full strength.

cards.title: A Blessing for Your Marriage
cards.text:
**Receive this blessing as you prepare to enter covenant.**

**May the God who brought you through grief bring you into joy.**

**May the love that did not end with death find new expression in this marriage.**

**May your covenant be strong enough to weather whatever storms come.**

**May your home be a place of peace, where faith is lived and love is practiced.**

**May your hearts be open to each other, vulnerable and protected at once.**

**May your memories of the past enrich rather than burden your future.**

**May your children, if you have them, find security in your union.**

**May your community support you and hold you accountable.**

**May your vows be kept, your love be sustained, your commitment be honored until the end.**

**And may the Lord bless you and keep you; may He make His face shine on you and be gracious to you; may He turn His face toward you and give you peace.**

**"The Lord bless you and keep you" (Numbers 6:24|The Lord bless you and keep you).** Be blessed. Be kept. Go forward with grace.

cards.title: Final Reflection
cards.text:
**As you stand on the threshold of this new covenant, reflect one more time.**

What are you most grateful for as you approach this marriage?

What hopes do you carry for your life together?

What wisdom will you bring from all you have experienced?

What commitment do you make, not just in vows but in daily intention?

What do you want to remember about this moment, standing on the edge of something new?
cards.reflection: What final reflections do you have as you prepare to enter this covenant?

cards.title: A Final Prayer
cards.text:
God,

**I am about to make a covenant.** I have prepared as best I can. Now I come to You.

**Thank You for bringing me through grief to this place.** Thank You for [partner's name]. Thank You for the gift of love again.

**I ask Your blessing on this marriage.** Be the foundation we build on. Be present in our home. Be the third strand in our cord.

**Help us keep the vows we make.** Help us love well, forgive quickly, and grow together. Help us honor You in how we treat each other.

**I commit this marriage to You.** Whatever comes, we will walk it with You. Whatever challenges arise, we will trust You through them.

**Bless this union.** Bless my partner. Bless any children in our family. Bless the years ahead.

**"For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh" (Ephesians 5:31|For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh).** Make us one, Lord. Make us Yours.

**In Jesus' name, Amen.**

**Write your own prayer if these words do not fit.**
cards.reflection: **Write your final prayer as you prepare to enter covenant.**

cards.title: Go Forward
cards.text:
**You are ready.**

**Not perfect.** Not without questions. Not certain of what the future holds.

**But ready.**

**You have done the work.** You have examined your heart. You have aligned with your partner. You have prepared with wisdom and faith.

**Now, go forward.**

**Make your vows with full intention.**

**Enter your covenant with eyes open.**

**Build your marriage on the foundation you have laid.**

**Trust God with what you cannot control.**

**Love well.** Forgive freely. Honor always.

**"And now these three remain: faith, hope and love. But the greatest of these is love" (1 Corinthians 13:13|And now these three remain: faith, hope and love.** But the greatest of these is love).

**Faith in the God who has brought you here.**

**Hope for the future He has for you.**

**Love, the greatest of these, which you are about to covenant again.**

Go. Be married. Be blessed.

**This is your new beginning.**
